Abstract 6

Conventional source- or nominal access-based indicators may overlook heterogeneity in the water-service 7

dimensions that shape everyday household experience, including reliability, affordability, accessibility, 8

quantity, acceptability, perceived quality, responsiveness, and household effort. We developed a household- 9

level Water Service Quality Score (WSQS) using 6,145 household surveys from South India. WSQS 10

integrates eight service domains and compares equal-, population-priority-, and individual-priority- 11

weighted formulations. We modeled WSQS using service-support, household-context, and stated-priority 12

predictors, evaluated performance across multiple predictive models, and interpreted predictions using 13

SHAP attribution and nonlinear service-response analyses. Within the fitted model, service-support 14

conditions accounted for most of the predictable variation and 94.9% of grouped SHAP attribution. 15

Important predictors included value for money, complaint resolution, water pressure, appearance 16

acceptability, water clarity, provider contact, and shortage experience. Household priorities contributed 17

modest, domain-specific heterogeneity but little incremental predictive performance.  These findings show 18

that household water service quality is multidimensional and measurable beyond access, helping water- 19

sector decision-makers identify and prioritize service deficiencies across heterogeneous provision systems. 20

Keywords: Water service quality; water infrastructure; household water security; heterogeneous water 21

provision; service delivery, water systems; user experience; priority-weighted measurement; machine 22

learning; SHAP 23

Introduction 24

Domestic water service in many low- and middle-income countries is rarely experienced through a single, 25

stable infrastructure pathway (Daly et al., 2021; Elliott et al. 2019). Although households are often classified 26

by their main or improved water source, everyday water use may depend on overlapping arrangements. 27

These sources may include piped supply, groundwater self-supply, tanker delivery, commercial water, 28

shared sources, rainwater harvesting, and other supplementary systems. A household may use one source 29

for drinking, another for cooking or washing, and shift between sources when supply becomes intermittent, 30

costly, insufficient, or mistrusted. This complicates monitoring because a primary-source category can 31

conceal the multiple arrangements households use to meet different needs. Systematic evidence from low- 32

and middle- income countries (LMIC) shows that multiple-source use is common, including among 33

households with improved primary sources, and unreliable supply can trigger storage, treatment, source 34

switching, and other coping strategies that reshape household service experience (Daly et al., 2021; Lee et 35

al., 2020). In these settings, source type is an incomplete proxy for service quality; for example, service 36

level may be measured through an established piped supply connection (Grafton et al., 2025; Geleijnse et 37

al., 2023). However, the same nominal source can produce very different experiences of reliability, 38

affordability, sufficiency, acceptability, and accessibility. 39

This creates a measurement problem for water-service monitoring. Conventional indicators, including 40

improved-source classifications, piped-connection status, and service ladders, remain essential for 41

comparison and planning, but they compress distinct dimensions of service into infrastructure-based 42

categories (Kayser et al., 2013; Vilarinho et al., 2024). Research on domestic water-service delivery has 43

long emphasized the need to monitor safety, quantity, accessibility, reliability, and cost rather than source 44

type alone (Kayser et al., 2013; Vilarinho et al., 2024; Hannah et al., 2020). Recent global mapping further 45

shows that even the use of safely managed drinking water remains data-limited across many LMICs 46


<!-- Page 3 -->


(Greenwood et al., 2024). At the household level, access and service quality can also diverge sharply; 47

evidence from Bangalore, India, shows that public-service access and piped-water service quality are 48

distinct outcomes shaped by institutional and political processes (Kumar et al., 2022). Monitoring 49

infrastructure access is therefore necessary, but it is not equivalent to measuring end-user service quality. 50

Household surveys provide one way to measure service dimensions that are often invisible in 51

infrastructure records, utility reports, or source classifications. They can capture pressure, interruptions, 52

shortages, cost burden, waiting time, perceived quality, acceptability, collection difficulty, satisfaction, and 53

provider responsiveness (Bazaanah et al., 2024; Osman and Faust, 2021; Hopkins et al., 2024; Hamilton et 54

al., 2024). Experience-based water insecurity research has shown that household water problems are 55

multidimensional and measurable across diverse LMIC contexts (Young et al., 2019). Related 56

methodological work emphasizes that micro-level water metrics must address dimensionality, temporality, 57

unit of analysis, and comparability, while also accounting for capabilities, institutions, governance, and 58

socio-cultural dynamics (Jepson et al., 2017; Wutich et al., 2017). Yet converting household survey 59

responses into a service-quality metric remains difficult. Survey items typically span physical, experiential, 60

institutional, and evaluative dimensions; they may operate on different ordinal scales; and they do not 61

necessarily contribute equally to overall service experience. A single satisfaction question may summarize 62

a household’s judgment, but it cannot diagnose whether poor service reflects unreliable supply, low 63

pressure, unaffordable cost, insufficient quantity, unacceptable quality, access burden, or weak customer 64

support. 65

Aggregation also raises a preference problem. A metric that combines affordability, access, reliability, 66

efficiency, acceptability, perceived quality, quantity sufficiency, and customer service must decide how to 67

weight those domains. Equal weighting provides a transparent baseline, but households may value service 68

dimensions differently. Stated-preference studies show heterogeneity in how households value 69

improvements in water quality, reliability, pressure, system management, and drinkability, while customer 70

satisfaction studies show that perceived health risk, organoleptic characteristics, payment systems, and price 71

shape service judgments (Rajapakshe et al., 2023; Vásquez et al., 2021; Denantes and Donoso, 2021; Ogata 72

et al., 2026). These findings suggest that priorities may shape how service conditions are interpreted, 73

weighted, and translated into overall service-quality judgments. At the same time, embedding stated 74

priorities directly into the modeled outcome can make later priority-based prediction circular. The 75

measurement challenge is therefore to retain a transparent and comparable service-quality metric while still 76

allowing household priorities to be examined as a source of heterogeneity in service experience. 77

Existing work has advanced several parts of this problem. Global monitoring studies provide standardized 78

indicators; household water insecurity scales measure lived water problems; multiple-source and coping 79

studies show how households respond to unreliable provision; satisfaction studies identify perceived 80

determinants of service experience; and customer-centered utility indices formalize service-quality 81

assessment at the provider level (Young et al., 2019; Daly et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2020; Denantes and 82

Donoso, 2021; Vilarinho et al., 2024; Skerker et al., 2026). Recent monitoring studies have also argued for 83

moving beyond isolated measurements, challenged narrow quantity-versus-quality framings, and linked 84

household water outcomes to tap-water service conditions (Charles et al., 2020; Nowicki et al., 2020; 85

Jeandron et al., 2019). What remains limited is an integrated household-level framework that combines 86

multiple domains of end-user service quality, compares priority-sensitive aggregation, and tests whether 87

household priorities add explanatory value beyond observed service conditions and household context. 88

We address this gap using survey data from 6,145 households in South India, primarily Tamil Nadu, where 89

households rely on heterogeneous water arrangements including piped supply, groundwater, tanker 90

delivery, and commercial water (Fig. 1). The Water Service Quality Score (WSQS) combines eight CORE- 91

8 domains: affordability, access, reliability, efficiency, acceptability, perceived quality, quantity 92

sufficiency, and customer service. We compare equal-weight, population-priority, and individual-priority 93

weighting architectures; assess item-level similarity using correlation and exploratory factor analysis; 94

model equal-weight WSQS using nested predictor sets; and evaluate whether household service quality is 95


<!-- Page 4 -->


explained primarily by operational service-support conditions, household context, or stated priorities. 96

Flexible predictive models are used diagnostically (not causally), and interpreted using SHAP attribution, 97

nonlinear response analysis, priority-conditioned contrasts, and robustness checks across outcome 98

definitions, model classes, context specifications, and repeated train-test splits. 99

The contribution of this paper is a household-level framework for measuring and diagnosing end-user 100

water service quality in heterogeneous provision systems. Existing household water-insecurity measures, 101

such as HWISE, quantify the severity of water-insecurity experiences (Young et al., 2019). WSQS instead 102

evaluates service performance and identifies the service dimensions in which deficiencies occur. The 103

framework moves beyond source type, infrastructure access, and single satisfaction measures; distinguishes 104

baseline measurement from priority-sensitive interpretation; tests whether priorities add information 105

beyond observed service conditions and household context; and identifies the physical, experiential, and 106

institutional conditions most strongly associated with household water service quality. It connects service- 107

quality measurement to broader efforts in water-service monitoring, water security, and equity-oriented 108

infrastructure assessment (Charles et al., 2020; Osman and Faust, 2021; Mohanavelu et al., 2024; 109

Mohanavelu and Osman, 2024; Savelli et al., 2023), while reframing monitoring from classifying access to 110

diagnosing how service functions in household experience. 111

3. Results 116

117

Multidimensional WSQS captures heterogeneity across service domains 118

The final WSQS construction dataset included 6,145 households. The Water Service Quality Score (WSQS) 119

was constructed from eight service-quality domains: affordability, access, reliability, efficiency, 120

acceptability, perceived quality, quantity sufficiency, and customer service. Each domain was harmonized 121

on a common direction-checked service-quality scale and transformed to the 0–100 reporting scale, where 122

higher values indicate better service quality (Fig. 2a). The domain response distributions showed substantial 123


<!-- Page 5 -->


variation across service dimensions, supporting the need for a multidimensional measure rather than a single 124

source-type, access, or satisfaction indicator (Fig. 2b; Table 1). 125

Mean domain scores ranged from 64.93 for acceptability to 76.08 for reliability on the 0–100 reporting 126

scale (Table 1). Quantity, access, and perceived quality also scored relatively high, with means of 75.52, 127

75.24, and 72.96, respectively. Efficiency was intermediate, with a mean of 71.22, while affordability and 128

customer service were both lower, with means of 68.83. This pattern indicates that households may report 129

relatively better reliability, quantity, access, or perceived quality, while still facing burdens in acceptability, 130

affordability, or customer service. These domain-level differences introduce the service-function 131

perspective developed throughout the paper. Rather than treating access or source type as a sufficient 132

summary, WSQS asks how well water service functions across the dimensions households experience. 133

Respondent-stated priorities also varied across domains (Fig. 2c; Table 2). These priorities were retained 134

on the original 0–10 scale and used to evaluate whether household-stated domain importance materially 135

changed WSQS measurement. The purpose of this comparison was not to replace the primary score with a 136

preference-weighted outcome, but to test whether priority weighting meaningfully changed the aggregate 137

distribution or individual household scores. 138

The three WSQS weighting architectures produced similar aggregate distributions. The equal-weight, 139

population-priority, and individual-priority WSQS means were 71.74, 71.74, and 71.77, respectively, on 140

the 0–100 reporting scale (Table 1). Individual-priority weighting shifted scores for some households, but 141

the aggregate shift was limited: the mean shift was 0.02 points, the median shift was 0.00, the mean absolute 142

shift was 0.95, the 95th percentile absolute shift was 3.71, and the correlation between equal-weight and 143

individual-priority WSQS was 0.991 (Fig. 2d; Table 3). These results support retaining equal-weight WSQS 144

as the primary non-circular modeling outcome, with population-priority and individual-priority WSQS 145

treated as sensitivity outcomes. 146

WSQS structure is coherent across domains and stable across weighting schemes 157

The domain correlation, quintile-profile, and weighting-robustness analyses were used to evaluate 158

complementary aspects of WSQS structure. Domain correlations tested whether the eight WSQS domains 159

were related enough to support aggregation, but not so highly correlated that they were redundant. Quintile 160

profiles tested whether the aggregate equal-weight WSQS ordered households coherently across the 161

underlying domains. Weighting comparisons tested whether the aggregate score was sensitive to equal, 162

population-priority, or individual-priority weighting. 163

Correlations among domain scores were generally positive, indicating that households reporting better 164

service in one domain also tended to report better service in other domains. However, the correlations were 165

moderate rather than near perfect. The correlation matrix showed values ranging from 0.12 to 0.52 outside 166

the diagonal, with the highest pairwise correlation observed between perceived quality and customer service 167

(Fig. 3a). This supports the interpretation of WSQS as a multidimensional index; the domains are related, 168

but each contributes distinct information. Supplementary measurement-structure diagnostics were 169

consistent with this interpretation. Exploratory factor analysis of the broader 32-item service-quality set 170

identified six empirical response factors rather than a one-to-one reproduction of the eight conceptually 171

specified WSQS domains. This is expected because the WSQS domains were specified as service-quality 172

dimensions for measurement and diagnosis, whereas the EFA was used descriptively to examine how 173


<!-- Page 8 -->


broader survey responses clustered empirically. The eight CORE-8 construction indicators nevertheless 174

showed moderate cross-domain coherence (Cronbach’s α = 0.757; Supplementary Information, Section 175

S1.3). Together, these results support treating WSQS as a multidimensional composite of related but non- 176

interchangeable service dimensions rather than as a unidimensional latent scale. 177

The quintile-profile analysis provided a second structural check. If the aggregate WSQS is meaningful, 178

households in higher WSQS quintiles should generally show better scores across the component domains. 179

This pattern was observed. The lowest equal-weight WSQS quintile had consistently lower domain scores, 180

while the highest quintile had substantially higher scores across nearly all domains (Fig. 3b). For example, 181

acceptability increased from 45.8 in the lowest quintile to 95.0 in the highest quintile, and customer service 182

increased from 45.9 to 93.4. The stronger gradients in the quintile-profile heatmap, compared with the more 183

moderate domain-correlation matrix, are informative as well. They indicate that domains are not redundant 184

at the item level, but they still move together sufficiently for the aggregate WSQS to separate lower- and 185

higher-service-quality households. 186

Our supplementary measurement diagnostics further supported the underlying WSQS structure. The 32 187

WSQS-related survey items showed excellent sampling adequacy (KMO = 0.937), significant factorability 188

(Bartlett’s χ²(496) = 40,065.6, p < 0.001), and substantial overall item-set coherence (Cronbach’s α = 189

0.850). Parallel analysis identified six empirical factors, while no highly correlated item pairs (|ρ| ≥ 0.80) 190

or problematic cross-loadings were observed. Together with the close agreement across weighting 191

architectures, these results indicate that the WSQS is both multidimensional and internally coherent, while 192

avoiding excessive redundancy among its constituent items (Supplementary Fig. S1; Supplementary Tables 193

S3–S4). 194

Distributional comparisons across weighting schemes provided the third structural check. The empirical 195

cumulative distribution functions for equal-weight, population-priority, and individual-priority WSQS 196

nearly overlapped (Fig. 3c), and pairwise agreement was high (Table 3). Equal-weight and population- 197

priority WSQS were nearly identical, with r = 1.000 and mean absolute difference of 0.14 points. 198

Individual-priority WSQS remained aligned with equal-weight WSQS, with r = 0.991 and mean absolute 199

difference of 0.95 points. These results show that priority weighting can shift some household scores 200

without destabilizing the aggregate WSQS distribution. Together, these structural checks justify using 201

equal-weight WSQS as the primary non-circular outcome and treating priority-weighted WSQS versions 202

as sensitivity outcomes. 203

Service-support variables explain most predictable variation in WSQS 215

Model performance was evaluated on the 20% test set, which was held out during model training. The 216

mean-only baseline had a test-set RMSE of 0.6389 on the raw 1–5 severity scale and explained essentially 217

no test-set variation (R² ≈ 0) (Fig. 4a,b; Table 4). Adding service-support variables produced the largest 218

improvement: the M1 service-support model reduced test-set RMSE to 0.4188 (Fig. 4a), increased test-set 219

R² to 0.570 (Fig. 4b), and achieved a Spearman rank correlation of approximately 0.748. 220


<!-- Page 10 -->


Adding household-context variables produced little additional improvement. The M2 model, which 221

included service-support and household context, had a test-set RMSE of 0.4187, R² of 0.571, and Spearman 222

ρ of approximately 0.749 (Fig. 4a,b; Table 4). Adding stated-priority variables in the final M3 model 223

produced a small additional gain: test-set RMSE decreased to 0.4179, R² increased to 0.572, and Spearman 224

ρ remained approximately 0.749 (Fig. 4a,b; Table 4). 225

This incremental priority signal is not mechanically induced by outcome construction. The primary 226

modeled outcome is the equal-weight WSQS, and stated priorities are not used to construct this primary 227

outcome. Priorities enter only as predictors in M3 and as weights in separate sensitivity outcomes. 228

Therefore, the M2-to-M3 comparison tests whether stated priorities explain residual variation in equal- 229

weight WSQS beyond service-support and context variables. 230

The observed-versus-predicted plot on the 0–100 reporting scale showed that the final M3 model preserved 231

the broad ordering of households by service quality, although prediction errors remained for individual 232

households (Fig. 4c). The final M3 model had a reporting-scale RMSE of 10.45, R² of 0.572, and Spearman 233

ρ of 0.749 (Fig. 4c). This nested model pattern supports two results. First, service-support conditions 234

contain most of the predictable information in equal-weight WSQS. Second, household context and stated 235

priorities add small but nonzero information beyond service-support variables, but the magnitude of these 236

additions is modest relative to the initial gain from service-support predictors. 237

Operational and institutional service conditions dominate model interpretation 246

The SHAP interpretation results confirmed that model predictions were dominated by operational and 247

institutional service-support variables. In the primary 20% test set, service-support variables accounted for 248

94.9% of total grouped mean absolute SHAP attribution, compared with 4.1% for stated priorities and 0.9% 249

for household context (Fig. 5a; Table 5). This pattern indicates that most prediction magnitude in the final 250

M3 model came from reported service-support conditions rather than household background variables or 251

stated priorities. 252

The highest-ranked individual predictors were also service-support variables. The leading predictors were 253

value for money, complaint resolution, water pressure, appearance acceptability, water clarity, provider 254

contact, shortage experience, quality change, backup reliability, taste acceptability, weekly water volume, 255

and disruption notice (Fig. 5b; Table 6). These predictors span both physical and institutional dimensions 256

of service: water pressure, clarity, quantity, shortages, and appearance describe direct service conditions, 257

while complaint resolution, provider contact, value for money, backup reliability, and disruption notice 258

capture responsiveness and service support. 259

This attribution pattern is important because it shows that WSQS variation was not explained primarily by 260

household context or stated priorities. Instead, the most significant signals were the operational and 261

institutional conditions through which households experienced water service. The grouped attribution result 262

should be interpreted as block-level predictive attribution rather than as a claim that every service-support 263

variable is individually more important than every context or priority variable. The robustness checks later 264

on further evaluate whether this pattern is stable across repeated data partitions. 265

Stated priorities add modest but interpretable heterogeneity 284

Although stated-priority variables contributed less than service-support variables overall, they provided a 285

small nonzero signal in the final M3 model. In the primary 20% test set, stated priorities accounted for 4.1% 286

of grouped SHAP attribution (Fig. 5a; Table 5). Because the primary outcome was equal-weight WSQS, 287

these priority contributions are non-circular; stated priorities were not used to construct the dependent 288

variable. Instead, they test whether households’ stated valuations of service domains explain additional 289

variation in equal-weight WSQS after observed service-support conditions and household context are 290

included. 291

Priority-conditioned service-response contrasts clarified where priorities modestly shaped model 292

predictions (Fig. 5c; Table 7). In the table and figure, the “×” symbol identifies the service condition and 293

the corresponding stated-priority dimension used for the contrast. Each contrast compares the predicted 294

service-response pattern for households with higher versus lower stated priority in the corresponding 295

domain. 296

Using the 0–100 WSQS service-loss scale, the largest priority-conditioned difference was for shortage 297

frequency × quantity priority: predicted service loss was 4.72 points among low-priority households and 298

4.25 points among high-priority households, yielding a high-minus-low difference of −0.47 points (Fig. 5c; 299

*Table 7). Odor acceptability × acceptability priority showed a smaller negative difference of −0.16 points. 300*

The remaining priority-conditioned differences were close to zero, ranging from 0.03 to 0.08 WSQS points 301

for appearance acceptability, taste acceptability, provider contact, available quantity, backup during failure, 302

and water clarity. These results indicate that stated priorities modestly condition selected service-response 303

patterns, but the differences are small relative to the main effects of service-support conditions. 304

Detailed priority-conditioned curves show the same pattern (Fig. 6a–d). Quantity, affordability, odor, and 305

appearance relationships differ slightly across low-, middle-, and high-priority groups, but the curves 306

remain close together. Thus, priorities refine interpretation but do not drive the model. The dominant 307

empirical signal remains the service condition itself, while priorities provide a smaller layer of 308

heterogeneity in how service conditions align with households’ stated importance. Extended predictor 309

rankings, service-priority pair definitions, nonlinear response summaries, and the survey-question map are 310

provided in Supplementary Section S3. 311

predicted WSQS changes unevenly across severity levels, but they do not establish causal patterns. 342

primarily by observed service-support conditions, with modest priority-conditioned heterogeneity. 344

This study develops a household-level framework for measuring end-user water service quality in 400

heterogeneous provision systems. The central finding is that household water service quality is 401

multidimensional, structured, and diagnosable. As summarized in Table 9, WSQS varied across 402

affordability, access, reliability, efficiency, acceptability, perceived quality, quantity sufficiency, and 403

customer service, confirming that source type, infrastructure access, or a single satisfaction question cannot 404

adequately represent household service quality. At the same time, individual-priority weighting shifted 405

some household scores but produced only limited aggregate change relative to the equal-weight score, with 406

a mean absolute difference of 0.95 points and a correlation of 0.991. For monitoring, this means that user 407

priorities can enrich interpretation without replacing a comparable baseline metric. Equal-weight WSQS 408

provides a stable reference point across households, while priority-weighted scores identify where 409

household values shift service-quality interpretation, especially in mixed-provision settings involving piped 410

supply, groundwater, tanker delivery, commercial water, and other sources. 411

A key contribution of the framework is that it separates measurement from preference sensitivity. Equal- 412

weight WSQS was retained as the primary outcome because it provides a transparent, non-circular baseline 413

with stated priorities not embedded in the dependent variable. Population-priority and individual-priority 414

scores were instead treated as sensitivity outcomes. Their similar aggregate distributions indicate that 415

WSQS is stable, while household-level shifts indicate that priorities still matter more to some respondents 416

than to others. This allows WSQS to remain comparable across households while preserving preference- 417

aware interpretation. 418

The primary empirical result is that WSQS is primarily structured by operational and institutional service- 419

support conditions. Adding service-support variables produced the main gain in prediction, while household 420

context and stated priorities added only small incremental improvements. SHAP attribution reinforced this 421

pattern, with service-support variables accounting for 94.9% of grouped attribution in the primary test set 422

and 93.2% across repeated splits. Thus, WSQS functions more as a service diagnostic than as a demographic 423

profiling tool. Specifically, household service quality is explained less by who households are than by the 424

service conditions they experience. 425

Next, the leading predictors broaden the scope of what counts as water service quality. Physical and 426

experiential conditions such as pressure, clarity, appearance, quantity, shortages, and taste mattered, but so 427

did institutional dimensions such as value for money, complaint resolution, provider contact, backup 428

reliability, disruption notice, and infrastructure maintenance. This shift monitoring beyond narrow quantity- 429

or quality-centered measures toward a more complete view of how households experience service delivery, 430

consistent with recent studies (Stoler et al. 2023; Pérez-Foguet, 2023; Fukuda et al., 2019). Further, 431

household context added limited independent signal once direct service-support conditions were measured. 432

This does not mean context is irrelevant; source type, income, household size, and dwelling conditions may 433

shape exposure to service constraints. Rather, the result suggests that these contextual differences or 434

inequities may operate through the operational conditions the model captures directly, such as pressure, 435

shortages, affordability burden, provider contact, and complaint resolution. Direct measurement of service 436

functioning is therefore more informative for diagnosing household-level water service quality than relying 437

on household characteristics or infrastructure categories alone as proxies. 438

Stated priorities added a modest but interpretable layer of heterogeneity. Because the primary modeled 439

outcome was an equal-weighted WSQS, this priority signal was not mechanically induced by priority- 440

weighted outcome construction. The findings suggest that priorities refined how selected service problems 441

were interpreted, especially when the priority domain aligned with the constrained service dimension. We 442

found no evidence that stated priorities replace operational service conditions as the main predictors of 443

WSQS. 444

Finally, the nonlinear response results further show why flexible, interpretable modeling is useful for this 445

problem. Water pressure, value for money, appearance acceptability, water clarity, and experience with 446

shortages showed the clearest nonlinear deterioration patterns. These findings suggest that service 447


<!-- Page 20 -->


deterioration may not be experienced as a smooth linear decline. For monitoring and planning, such patterns 448

matter because average or linear summaries can obscure the points at which worsening service conditions 449

produce sharper losses in household service quality. Also, the robustness checks strengthen the main 450

interpretation. As summarized in Table 9, the same pattern held across weighting schemes, repeated train- 451

test splits, benchmark learners, context encodings, and grouped attribution checks. This suggests that the 452

results are not artifacts of a single weighting choice, model class, data split, or attribution method. 453

Several limitations remain in this work. The analysis is cross-sectional and predictive, not causal. Because 454

all survey-based outcome and predictor measures were reported by the same household respondent, 455

associations may partly reflect shared reporting tendencies as well as underlying service conditions. WSQS 456

relies on self-reported household service experience and stated priorities, which may reflect recall, 457

expectations, or reporting differences. Perceived water quality was measured through household experience 458

rather than laboratory testing, so WSQS should complement, not replace, chemical or microbiological 459

safety monitoring. The survey used a non-probability, purposive maximum-variation recruitment strategy; 460

results should therefore not be interpreted as population-weighted prevalence estimates for a bounded 461

geography. External validation is needed before transferring the calibrated model or weights to other 462

regions or provision contexts. 463

Overall, the study shows that end-user water service quality in heterogeneous provision systems is 464

multidimensional, operationally structured, modestly priority-conditioned, and robust across modeling 465

choices. For water-service monitoring in LMICs and heterogeneous provision systems, this shifts 466

the question from whether households have access to water to how well that service functions from the 467

user’s perspective. 468

Methods 470

Study design and analytical workflow 471

This study developed a household-level measurement and predictive modeling framework for end-user 472

water service quality in heterogeneous water provision systems. The objective was to test whether a 473

multidimensional Water Service Quality Score (WSQS) could represent household service experience more 474

comprehensively than source type, infrastructure access, or a single satisfaction measure. 475

The workflow included (i) survey quality assurance, (ii) response harmonization, (iii) construction of the 476

CORE-8 WSQS, (iv) comparison of alternative weighting architectures, (v) predictive modeling with 477

service-support, household-context, and stated-priority variables, and (vi) model interpretation through 478

SHAP, nonlinear response analysis, and robustness checks. The analysis was designed as a predictive and 479

diagnostic modeling exercise, not as a causal treatment-effect study. Estimated relationships are therefore 480

interpreted as associations between observed household service conditions, stated priorities, household 481

context, and WSQS. 482


<!-- Page 22 -->


Study setting, sampling strategy, survey administration, and consent 483

The study used household survey data collected primarily in Tamil Nadu, South India, where domestic 484

water service is provided through heterogeneous arrangements including piped supply, groundwater, tanker 485

delivery, commercially purchased water, and combinations of primary and supplementary sources. The 486

household was the unit of analysis. Adult respondents (≥18 years) served as household informants, 487

reporting on household water-service conditions, constraints, coping arrangements, and priorities. This use 488

of an adult household informant is consistent with established household-survey practice, including major 489

international household surveys that collect household-level water and sanitation information through an 490

adult household member (UNICEF MICS, 2018). Primary household data were necessary because source 491

classification and nominal infrastructure access alone do not jointly capture experienced dimensions of 492

service such as affordability, sufficiency, acceptability, and responsiveness (Chen et al., 2017; Omarova et 493

al., 2019). 494

The survey used a non-probability, purposive maximum-variation recruitment strategy to obtain broad 495

coverage of contrasting water-service conditions and provision arrangements (Palinkas et al., 2015; Penrod 496

et al., 2003; Platt et al., 2006). Recruitment was conducted by the study investigator through supervised, 497

investigator-administered field access, with local institutional partners facilitating access to potential 498

participants and study communities. Structured chain-referral recruitment extended participation beyond 499

the initial access points. The resulting household sample included respondents reporting on a range of 500

water-provision arrangements and socioeconomic conditions, including formal, self-supplied, purchased, 501

and supplementary water systems. Recruitment through multiple supervised access pathways broadly 502

followed the community-based household survey approaches described by Cooper et al. (2023), Banerji et 503

al. (2013), and Hori et al. (2013). Local institutional partners facilitated field access and recruitment but did 504

not define the analytical population. 505

This sampling design was selected to capture heterogeneity in household water-service experience rather 506

than to estimate population prevalence. Because individual inclusion probabilities were unknown, the study 507

does not make design-based population estimates for Tamil Nadu. Analyses therefore focus on 508

measurement structure, heterogeneity in observed household service conditions, and predictive 509

relationships across the water-service configurations represented in the dataset. Respondent characteristics 510

are treated as descriptive attributes of the household informants rather than as the inferential target of the 511

study. The Supplementary Information (Section S4) provides an independent sample-coverage and 512

external-benchmark diagnostic, characterizing household composition, socioeconomic indicators, 513

geographic reach and recruitment concentration, rural–urban settlement context, population-density 514

coverage, and the diversity of domestic water-provision arrangements represented in the study. These 515

diagnostics clarify the empirical breadth of the sample while transparently distinguishing observed 516

coverage from probability-based representativeness. 517

Survey deployment was preceded by a pilot involving 266 participants approximately one week before 518

full-scale field deployment. The pilot assessed question comprehension, response-option clarity, survey 519

flow, accessibility, and administration procedures, and the findings were used to refine the finalized field 520

instrument before deployment (Presser et al., 2004; Willis, 2005; Groves et al., 2009). Translated versions 521

used during field administration were also reviewed and piloted before deployment. During the main study, 522

surveys were investigator-administered using a standardized instrument and supervised field procedures. 523

Stanford University Institutional Review Board reviewed and approved the study protocol (protocol no. 524

82168) before data collection. All respondents were aged 18 years or older and provided electronic 525

informed consent before participation. Participation was voluntary, and responses were de-identified before 526

analysis. 527

Survey records were screened before analysis using pre-specified quality-assurance rules. Records were 529

retained only if they had sufficient completion, valid consent and eligibility information, interpretable 530

Survey measures 539

The survey captured four groups of variables. Specifically, first, CORE-8 service-quality items were used 540

to construct WSQS across eight domains: affordability, access, reliability, efficiency, acceptability, 541

perceived quality, quantity sufficiency, and customer service. One broad item from each domain was used 542

Robustness and sensitivity analyses 684

Robustness checks evaluated whether the main conclusions were sensitive to data partitioning, model class, 685

outcome definition, context specification, or attribution procedure. First, repeated train-test splits tested 686

whether the nested model pattern depended on a single favorable partition. Second, benchmark models 687

tested whether the results were specific to CatBoost. Third, the final M3 predictor set was evaluated across 688

equal-weight, population-priority, and individual-priority WSQS outcomes. Fourth, context-specification 689

checks compared the main context block with fuller context and alternative income encodings. Finally, 690

repeated-split grouped SHAP analyses tested whether the service-support attribution pattern remained 691

stable across data partitions. 692

Reporting convention and inference 693

Two WSQS scales were used. Model fitting, validation, SHAP attribution, and nonlinear response analyses 694

were conducted on the raw 1–5 severity scale, where lower values indicate better service quality. 695

Descriptive domain and aggregate WSQS summaries were reported on the transformed 0–100 scale, where 696

higher values indicate better service quality. Priority-conditioned service-loss contrasts were also reported 697

on the 0–100 WSQS scale to aid interpretation. All figures and tables identify whether values are reported 698

on the raw severity scale or the 0–100 reporting scale. 699

All results should be interpreted as predictive and diagnostic. The sampling strategy supports analysis of 700

measurement structure and service-quality relationships within a heterogeneous household dataset, but it 701

does not support population-weighted prevalence claims for Tamil Nadu or any bounded administrative 702

unit. External validation is required before transferring calibrated weights, predictor effects, or model 703

performance estimates to other regions or provision contexts. 704
